paragraphs.text: A [Meizhan](yancha:meizhan) [oolong](oolong:definition) made in 2004, partly oxidised to a medium degree and finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making), the roast that dries the leaf so it keeps. Meizhan is a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi and is also made in the Wuyi way, though it is less famous than Rougui and Shui Xian and is not one of the four famous bushes.

The leaf comes from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), on Fujian's border with Jiangxi. Here bushes grow slowly in thin, stony soil on ledges and in ravines, under heavy rain and frequent fog. The record names no [zone](wuyi-mountains:zones), so it does not say how close to the rocky core of the range this tea grew.

Twenty-two years have passed since it was made. Roasted Wuyi tea is the kind [kept for years](yancha:ageing), and its keeping depends on staying sealed and dry, because damp is what turns stored leaf back toward going green, the main fault of age.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker liquor with less sharpness, the roast softened and the high aroma faded.
